title.analysis: Authentic title "The 3 Income Levels Where Life Starts Feeling Different" is a framework-promise frame. The script delivers three levels defined by fears (drowning, decision tax, paycheck dependence); level three is defined by assets rather than income, which the script acknowledges.

thumbnail.analysis: Registered maxresdefault 1280x720 (HTTP 200, real image). Three white panels: "$50K" over the recurring cartoon man in torn clothes beside a rusted car, "$250K" over him in a polo beside a silver Toyota sedan, "$1M" over him in a suit and sunglasses beside a red Ferrari and a woman in an evening dress. At 320x180 all three numbers and figures read clearly. The thresholds ($50K/$250K/$1M) do not match the script's levels (about $50-60K, about $118K, and about $2M of assets), and the luxury-car level contradicts the script's "not a yacht" quiet-freedom message.

script.opening_words: You're standing in the grocery store with that little running total going in your head, not because you're some budgeting savant who color code spreadsheets, because you genuinely don't know if the card's going to go through. So, you put the name brand cereal back. You walk past the meat counter like you weren't going to buy any anyway. You decide you don't really like avocados. Then, one day, years later, you're in that same store and you realize you
script.ending_words: be. First you stop drowning, then you stop deciding. Then if you guard that gap patiently enough, you stop depending, and your money quietly starts buying back your afternoons. That's the level actually worth chasing, not the one with the biggest number on it, the one where the only math you've got left is figuring out how you want to spend a Tuesday. I'll see you in the next one.
script.analysis: Full 18318 canonical characters read. A single-narrator framework essay with a composite (Kyla, a single parent rising from $46,000 to $58,000 to $118,000 to financial independence): level one (emergency buffer; Fed SHED, median income, state gaps), level two (decision tax; happiness-income research, costs of children, insurance, housing, take-home pay), level three (assets; percentiles, 4% rule, stock ownership), the lifestyle-creep objection, and a callback close. Research citations are mostly accurate; the Texas take-home figure is about $5,000 low and several statistics are unsourced.
